plan.paradox: A bundle wins, even though a cheaper plan looks cheaper.
plan.odd_fact: Print-only never gets chosen, yet it's listed alongside the bundle.
plan.twist: The unused print-only option works as a decoy.
plan.cause: The $125 print-only option, priced the same as the bundle but offering less, pushes students toward the $125 bundle (84% choose it). Removing it drops bundle choice to 32% and raises the $59 web plan to 68%.
plan.everyday: A bakery offers plain croissant $2, chocolate croissant $3, almond croissant $3; the almond croissant serves as a decoy, making the chocolate croissant feel like the smart pick.
plan.rule: If an option never gets chosen, it's probably a decoy. Follow for more.

title: A Bundle Wins, Even Though a Cheaper Plan Looks Cheaper
caption: See how a useless option can steer choices. Follow for more price tricks!

beats.say: A bundle wins, even though a cheaper plan looks cheaper.
Print-only, same price as the full package, no web.
Web-only, digital access for less money.
Print plus web, full experience for the same price as print-only.
Nobody ever picks print-only. Looks useless.
But it's a decoy that pushes the bundle.
With the decoy present, 84 of 100 students choose the bundle.
Take away the $125 print-only and the bundle drops to 32, while the $59 web plan climbs to 68.
Now $125 feels like a bargain because the alternative looks the same but offers less.
You see it everywhere. A bakery lists plain croissant $2, chocolate croissant $3, almond croissant $3.
Now the $3 chocolate croissant feels smart, because the $3 almond one adds nothing extra.
If nothing ever chooses an option, suspect a decoy. Follow for more.
